title: Piano Sonata No. 11 in A major
hook: A gentle tune in six disguises, a graceful minuet, and the “Turkish” finale everyone can hum.

painting.title: Cornelis Calkoen on his Way to his Audience with Sultan Ahmed III
painting.pairingNote: Janissaries, the Ottoman sultan’s elite soldiers, throw themselves at dishes of rice in a courtyard of the Topkapı Palace; the military bands of these same soldiers were what Vienna’s “Turkish” fashion, and Mozart’s finale, set out to imitate.

facts: Mozart probably wrote it in the early 1780s, most likely in Vienna; scholars long dated it to 1783, though the latest research suggests it may be a little earlier. It was published in Vienna in August 1784, together with the Sonatas K. 330 and K. 332.

It breaks the usual pattern. None of its three movements is in [[sonata-form|sonata form]]: it opens with a theme and variations, continues with a [[minuet|minuet]], and ends with a [[rondo|rondo]]. All three stay in A, major or minor.

The finale imitates the bands of the Janissaries, the Ottoman sultan’s soldiers, with their drums, cymbals and shrill pipes. “Turkish” music was the height of fashion in Vienna; Mozart’s opera *The Abduction from the Seraglio*, a hit in 1782, has two Janissary choruses.

For two centuries only the last page of Mozart’s manuscript was known. In 2014 a librarian in Budapest, Balázs Mikusi, found four more pages, and the pianist Zoltán Kocsis played the newly found text there that September.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a tune in six disguises (I), a graceful dance (II), a march with an imaginary drum (III).

movements.heading: Andante grazioso
movements.summary: A gentle, swaying tune followed by six [[variation|variation]]s. Each variation keeps the tune’s shape and length but changes its clothes: new rhythms, a turn to the minor, a slow, ornate version, and a fast, brilliant ending.

mainIdeas.name: The theme
mainIdeas.description: a calm, rocking tune in 6/8, in the lilting rhythm of a [[siciliano|siciliano]]. Two short halves, each played twice.

mainIdeas.name: The variations
mainIdeas.description: six new versions of the same tune, each a little world of its own.

stops.hear: A calm, rocking melody in the right hand over soft chords
The tune broken into short notes, with small leaning notes that sigh against the harmony
The left hand ripples in quick groups of three under a decorated tune
Darker: the tune in the minor, in smooth lines of octaves
Back in the major, soft; the left hand crosses over the right to play high notes
Slow and richly ornamented, with fast flourishes around the tune
Fast and bright, now in four beats instead of a lilt, ending with a short flourish

notice: Try to hum the theme through each variation. Its shape is always there, even when it is buried in fast notes.
Variation 6 changes the metre: the rocking six becomes a brisk four, the clearest sign that the end is near.

movements.heading: Menuetto
movements.summary: A stately [[minuet|minuet]] with wide-spaced chords and sudden loud and soft contrasts. The [[trio|trio]] in the middle is gentler and moves to D major, with the hands crossing over each other.

mainIdeas.name: The minuet
mainIdeas.description: firm chords and octaves, graceful but grand.

mainIdeas.name: The trio
mainIdeas.description: a softer, singing tune in D major; the left hand reaches over the right.

stops.hear: Firm, spacious chords and octaves in a measured three-beat dance
The dance moves further away, with sudden quiet answers to loud phrases
Softer and warmer, in a new key; the left hand crosses over to add notes above the right
The trio’s second half, also played twice
The firm chords of the opening return

notice: Watch for the hand-crossing in the trio, if you are watching a pianist: the left hand jumps over the right to play the higher notes.

movements.heading: Alla turca. Allegretto
movements.summary: The famous “Turkish” finale. A quick, nimble tune in A minor alternates with a loud, stamping march in A major, where the left hand’s rolled chords imitate the crash of cymbals and drums. It is a [[rondo|rondo]]: the march keeps coming back.

mainIdeas.name: The minor tune
mainIdeas.description: quick notes turning around a single note, light and nimble.

mainIdeas.name: The march
mainIdeas.description: loud, in octaves, over rolled chords in the left hand, the “Janissary” sound.

mainIdeas.name: The coda
mainIdeas.description: the march’s rhythm hammered out, with the rolled chords at full force.

stops.hear: A quick tune in the minor, circling around one note
stops.happening: The opening tune, in A minor

stops.hear: Loud and bright: a march in octaves, with rolled, crashing chords in the left hand
stops.happening: The refrain, in A major. Cymbals and drums, imagined on the piano

stops.hear: Running fast notes over broken chords, in a darker key
The nimble minor tune once more
The march, for the third time
Hammered rhythm and crashing chords, then loud, final octaves

notice: Listen to the left hand in the march. The rolled chords, struck fast from bottom to top, are Mozart’s way of making a piano sound like a Janissary band.

notes.title: Mozart’s own word
notes.body: The early sources mark this movement *Allegrino*, “a little lively”, an unusual word; the heading “Alla turca” appears to have been added when the sonata was printed. Pianos with a “Janissary stop”, a pedal that worked a drum, cymbals and a triangle, were built only later, in the 19th century. Mozart’s drum is in the notes themselves.

threads.title: One key
threads.body: All three movements stay in A major or A minor. Variety comes from rhythm and colour, not from changing key.

threads.title: Disguises
threads.body: The first movement dresses one tune six ways; the finale turns the piano into a military band.

threads.title: Two hands
threads.body: In the fourth variation and in the trio the left hand crosses over the right; in the finale it becomes the drummer.
